opener.heading: Week 14: Egg-cellent Science 🥚
about: One object, seven days. She paints six eggs on Friday, stacks a pile of books on four eggshells on Saturday, shuffles one along the hall on the tops of her feet like a penguin on Sunday, and lifts two out of a vinegar jar with the shells eaten off them on Monday. The egg is strong, fragile, cheap, edible and the right size for her hand, and every day this week takes it apart another way.

No holiday lands in these seven days. Easter was last Sunday, so the eggs on the table are the plain kind. Monday the 5th carries the month's calendar work: April's handprint goes up beside January's, Azlyn gets a fresh pencil mark on the door frame, and Kreston turns 10 months and gets his first line four below hers. Friday opens the week with a second new year, six painted eggs standing on the dinner table and a new set of questions taped to the shelf beside the January time capsule.
azlyn: A dome carries weight. Four eggshells hold a stack of books, then cave under one thumb the other way up.
Real size at real scale. Six eggs drawn true to size, hummingbird to ostrich, taped along the hall floor and walked.
Sorting by a rule the object doesn't show. Feathers, fur, scales and six legs cut clean across color.
Wax and oil push water off. On a shell, on paper, on her coat in the rain, and in a jar she shakes herself.
Cracking, whisking and cooking. Twelve eggs on Saturday, then her own fork and her own pan on Thursday with your hand over hers.
you: Two new years in one book is a useful idea
Sanctioned rule-breaking is good for a rule-following child
Trying and failing at something an animal does easily builds real respect
Children can't perceive their own growth, and showing it matters
Sorting into families is a more advanced move than sorting by color
Resist techniques teach a real idea: some things repel others
Doing your own version beside her beats helping with hers
shopping: Eggs, 40 across the week, one box of them the cheapest in the store
A quail egg, or a large dried lima bean as the stand-in
White vinegar, a large bottle
Food coloring, 4 colors
Washable non-toxic poster paint in 4 colors
Corn syrup (or 6 tablespoons of salt), plus salt for the dressing
Cooking oil, soy sauce, sugar and a tablespoon of milk
Dried pasta and uncooked rice
All-purpose flour, enough to fill a tray
A lettuce
Dish soap
Paper towels
Empty egg cartons, 3
Trays, 3
Large mixing bowls, 2
Small bowls, 6, two or three of them shallow
Mugs, 4
Clean jars, 5, at least two with lids
A small bottle with a tight lid, for the dressing
A whisk and 3 forks
A slotted spoon and a teaspoon
Clothespins, 2, and kitchen tongs
A drinking straw
Small non-stick frying pans, 2, or one and take turns
A spatula, a chopping board, 2 plates and a knife (yours only)
Paper, 30 sheets
Thick card, 5 sheets, one of them stiff enough to take a stack of books
Crayons, including a white wax crayon and a dark one with the paper off
A stub of white candle
Masking tape, 2 rolls
Poster putty
A permanent marker and a pencil
A ruler and a measuring tape
Child-safe scissors, and your own pair for the string
A glue stick and a stapler
An envelope
Chalk, the fat sidewalk kind
An old magazine or a supermarket catalog
Paper plates, 4, or four more sheets of paper
String or thick wool, 1 ball
A wide soft brush and a narrow brush
Books of a similar size, 10–15
Her animal toys, 15–20
An old towel for the floor, and a folded towel for the shuffle course
An apron or an old shirt
A wet washcloth, a cloth for the table and hand soap at the sink
A rolled pair of socks
A flashlight with fresh batteries
January's handprint sheet, down off the wall
Your phone, for the drop timer, Friday's answers and Thursday's photos
opener.krestonNote: Kreston is 9 months this week. He pulls to stand on anything at knee height, picks up single small things between finger and thumb, and waves at every face he passes. He turns 10 months on Monday the 5th, and starts cruising the furniture, pointing at what he wants, and stopping when you say no.

days.title: The Second New Year
days.prepTonight: Boil six eggs, cool them under the cold tap and leave them in the fridge, then cut the lid off an empty egg carton and stand the base on a tray with the paints.

opening.title: One Egg Each
opening.need: the 6 cooled hard-boiled eggs · 1 permanent marker · 1 tray.
steps: Put the cold eggs on the table and count the people in the house with her. Four, and two spares for the ones that crack. If nothing got boiled last night, put six on now and count the names while they cook, then cool them under the cold tap.
She hands one egg to each name out loud. Write the first letter on each base with the marker while she decides whose is whose.
Line them up on the tray. Every one gets painted at 9:15.

main.title: The Spring New Year Table
materials: Washable non-toxic poster paint in 4 colors
1 empty egg carton, cut down, as a drying rack
steps: Paper towels over the table, the cut-down carton at one end as the drying rack, the four paints in a row.
She starts with her own egg. Wide brush, one whole color, then straight into a hole in the carton to dry while she does the next.
Once all six have a base color, hand her the narrow brush. Spots, stripes, a face, whatever belongs to the person the egg is for. She decides what Kreston's looks like.
Paint one yourself while she works, and take her instructions on it.
When they are dry to the touch, turn each over and write the name in marker beside the letter.
Stand all six on the tray in the middle of the dinner table. They stay there until she is done with them.
main.tip: Persian families have kept a table like this for three thousand years, one painted egg for every person in the house. Tell her that while she paints.

outside.title: Watching for Nesting Birds
paras: Birds are building all over the street in the first week of April, and this morning she supplies them. Cut a dozen short lengths of wool, none longer than her thumb, and let her drape them over a low shrub, a fence wire and the gate latch. Add a pinch of moss and the hair off her brush. Count what she leaves out, and come back before dinner to count what is gone.

days.infant: Kreston is 9 months and picks up single small things between finger and thumb. Give him the lid you cut off the egg carton and let him work the hinge with that new grip while Azlyn paints. On the walk he waves at everyone, so face him outward.

second.title: The Spring Questions
second.intro: The time capsule has sat sealed on the high shelf since New Year's Day. Three months on, she answers a second set of questions and they go up beside it.
materials: Your phone, to photograph the answers
steps: Show her the sealed box on the shelf first, and tell her when it comes back down.
One question per sheet, written across the top in pencil: favorite color, favorite food, best thing about Kreston, what she wants to do when it gets warm.
Write her answer underneath word for word. If she gives you a story instead of an answer, take the story.
Read all four back to her in her own words and let her correct you.
Turn the fourth sheet over. Crayons, and she draws everyone in the house, Kreston included.
Photograph all four sheets before they go anywhere near the envelope.
Fold them in, let her seal it and scribble on the front, then write OPEN DECEMBER 31 across it and tape it to the shelf edge beside the box.
second.tip: Resist steering her toward a better answer. The version you want to read in December is the one where she says her favorite food is ice cubes.

alternatives: Questions only. Skip the envelope and stick the sheets on the fridge.
Draw the family on one big sheet and stop there.
Look back at January's photos and name who is in each one.
Let her interview you, and write your answers down the same way.
outAgain: Meet a friend at the park, and take two painted eggs to show
The green with a ball, if the friend falls through
A café with a window and something to watch
The long way round, to see whether the wool has gone off the fence
A drive out to see the blossom before the wind takes it

aroundWorld.title: Japan, Tamagoyaki 🍳
paras: Japanese cooks make tamagoyaki in a small rectangular pan, pouring egg in thin layers and rolling each new one onto the last until the omelette is a block of ten or twelve layers. It goes into lunch boxes cold, cut into slices that show every layer. Tokyo cooks sweeten theirs with sugar. Osaka cooks leave it savory.
aroundWorld.tryIt: You cook it on Thursday, in two pans, one each. Until then, cut a slice of any omelette and count the layers with her. There is one.
aroundWorld.didYouKnow: Sushi masters once judged an apprentice on his tamagoyaki before letting him near the fish.

days.krestonPM: He gets his handprint and his height on the wall on Monday, so today he sits in on the questions. Put him on the floor by the table with a sheet of paper of his own. At 9 months he tears, crumples and tastes it. Say his name in her answers out loud.

insight.headline: Two new years in one book is a useful idea.
paras: Azlyn has no working sense of a year. January 1 meant nothing to her beyond the noise, and December is not a place she can picture. What she can hold is a thing that comes round again. Marking a second new year this spring, with the Persian Nowruz behind us, the Thai and Cambodian new years in the middle of this month, and the blossom outside, gives her a second run at the same idea while the evidence is on the trees. Repeat the ritual and she gets time as a circle before she ever gets it as a number. Six painted eggs on the dinner table do that work for you all week.

days.safety: You boil the eggs tonight while Kreston is up. At 9 months he pulls to stand on anything at knee height, including the oven door, so he stays out of the kitchen the whole time the pan is on the stovetop. A chunk of hard-boiled egg is the exact size that blocks his airway. Count the eggs onto the tray and count them back. The painted eggs stand on the table all week as decoration, so nobody eats one.

days.title: How Strong Is an Egg
days.prepTonight: Crack four eggs into a bowl for the morning, keeping the halves whole, then rinse them and even the rims off with your thumbnail so each one stands level.

opening.title: Squeezing the Egg
opening.need: 1 raw egg · 1 large mixing bowl · soap and a towel at the sink.
steps: Hold the egg down in the bowl and squeeze it in your whole fist, hard, no fingernails and no thumb on one spot. It holds.
Her turn. She will not break it, and will not believe that until she has tried three times.
Now tap the same egg once on the rim. Ask her why one hand could not do what one tap did, and leave her answer until 9:15. Soap and the towel at the sink first.

main.title: The Books on the Eggshells
materials: 4 empty half eggshells with the rims trimmed level
1 flat piece of thick card or a chopping board
Paper and a marker for the count
steps: Stand the four shells dome side up on the tray in a rectangle the size of the board, each stuck down with a curl of masking tape.
Lay the board flat across all four. Press the middle with one finger and let her feel that nothing moves.
First book on, flat and central. She places every one from here. Write 1 on the paper.
One book at a time, counting out loud and writing each number as it lands. Past eight she will start whispering.
When a shell goes, it goes with a crack and no warning. Circle the number that broke it.
Turn the surviving shells the other way up, dome down, and press one with a thumb. It caves at once.
main.tip: The dome sends the weight down the curve to the rim instead of into one spot. Say it after she has watched it happen.

outside.title: The Blossom Walk
paras: Early April is the two weeks the blossom is out and the wind is waiting for it. Stand under the loudest tree on your street. Cherry is pink and frilled, crabapple deeper and a week or two behind it, redbud purple straight off the bare wood, and all of them snow when the wind gets up. Let her catch petals, then collect five off the ground, one from under each different tree.

days.infant: Kreston is 9 months and pulls to stand on anything that holds him. Give him two books off the pile at floor level and let him haul himself up on the sofa. The eggshells and the tray stay on the table. Under the blossom, hold him up to a low branch.

second.title: Permission to Smash
second.intro: A dozen of the cheapest eggs in the store and one instruction: break them. She has spent three months hearing you say be careful.
materials: Warm soapy water and a cloth
steps: Towel under the table, apron on her, both mixing bowls and the shallow bowl in her reach.
Hand her the box. Eggs into the first bowl any way she likes, and say nothing about technique for the first eight.
Shells go into the shallow bowl as she goes. That is the one rule.
Keep the last four back. Crack each one and tip the yolk from half shell to half shell, letting the white run into the second bowl. Give her the fourth.
Whisk in her hand, second bowl in your lap. Clear, then cloudy, then white, then a foam that holds the whisk's shape.
Dip the fork in and lift it. A peak stands up on the tines and stays there.
Warm soapy water and the cloth. She does the table, you do the floor, everybody does hands.
second.tip: Eight eggs make a large omelette or tomorrow's pancakes. Say that out loud at the start.

alternatives: Six eggs instead of twelve, straight into the pan.
Whisk dishwater bubbles in the sink and skip the eggs.
Crack them outside on the step, into a bucket.
Meringue, if the foam has come out well enough to bake.
outAgain: The museum, first Saturday of the month
Whichever room has bones, eggs or birds in it, and skip the rest
Indoor playground if the line is out of the door
The park bench by the blossom tree from this morning
The garden center, for the bird feeders and the seedlings
days.krestonPM: He comes to the museum in the carrier. At 9 months a big echoing room is a lot of work, so twenty minutes up high facing out, then a carpeted corner where he can pull up on a bench. Let Azlyn pick the room he sees.

insight.headline: Sanctioned rule-breaking is good for a rule-following child.
paras: Azlyn has spent the winter learning what she must not do with the good plates, the wall and the eggs. Handing her twelve eggs and permission to destroy them does not undo that, because the permission comes with a boundary she can see: this box, this bowl, this table. She gets to run the destructive impulse inside a frame you built. Children who get sanctioned outlets for the wild end of themselves push less at the edges of everything else, and she learns that a rule has a shape and an inside. Say the yes out loud and mean it.

days.safety: Raw egg carries salmonella and it will be on her hands, the table and the floor. Soap and warm water before anyone touches Kreston, the snack or a tap handle. Wipe drips as they land, because a wet floor is a fall for Kreston hauling himself upright on furniture. Broken shell has an edge on it, and he now picks up single small things and puts them in his mouth, so the shell bowl stays on the table.

days.title: The Penguin Job
days.prepTonight: Boil three eggs for the fridge and snip a length of string into short worms for the afternoon. Stand two raw eggs in a jar, cover them with white vinegar and push it to the back of the counter until Monday morning.

schedule.label: Quiet Play
schedule.name: The Bird Book on the Sofa

schedule.label: Wind-Down
schedule.name: Low Light and a Long Story

opening.title: No Hands Allowed
opening.need: masking tape · 1 rolled pair of socks.
steps: Run a strip of masking tape down the hall floor, three or four meters.
Walk the line together, feet turned out, arms flat at your sides. No arms from here on.
Balance the rolled socks on the tops of her feet and let her shuffle the line without dropping them. See how far she gets before they land.

main.title: The Penguin Shuffle
materials: Masking tape for the course line
1 folded towel as the landing pad
A stopwatch or the phone timer
Paper and a marker for the drop count
steps: This morning's tape line is the course. A fresh strip of masking tape across the far end is the finish, and the folded towel down the middle is the landing pad.
Egg on the tops of her feet, ankles together, hands off. She shuffles the line without lifting a foot off the floor.
Every drop gets a stroke on the paper in marker. Do not comment on them.
Time how long she can hold one egg standing still. A male emperor penguin does it for two months in the dark at forty below, without eating.
The hand-off: she shuffles the egg onto your feet and you shuffle it back, hands behind your backs. Real penguins lose eggs here too.
Run the course with all three eggs at once if she is still in it. Count the survivors.
main.tip: She will want to use her hands, so give them a job. Have her hold her own elbows.

outside.title: The Waddle to the Corner
paras: Walk to the end of the road the way the birds do. Penguin: feet out, arms flat, tiny steps. Duck: same feet, lower. Heron: one slow leg at a time, knees high. Pigeon: head forward and back with every step, which she does better than you. Let her call the changes.

days.infant: Kreston is 9 months and waves at anything with a face. Sit him on a cushion past the finish line so Azlyn shuffles toward him and gets a wave each time she arrives. The eggs go back in the box between runs, because loose on the floor they are the size he chokes on.

second.title: Four Kinds of Beak
second.intro: Four tools and four kinds of dinner. Every beak in the yard handles one and fails at the other three.
materials: Kitchen tongs, or a second clothespin
1 shallow bowl of water with torn lettuce floating in it
String cut into short worms, buried in a tray of flour
steps: Four stations along the table: dried pasta in one bowl, rice in a second, the shallow bowl of water with the lettuce on top, and the flour tray with the string worms buried in it.
The last two small bowls are the stomachs, hers and yours. Everything caught goes in.
Lay the beaks out: a clothespin each, the teaspoon, the straw, the tongs. She tries one on all four foods before swapping.
The clothespin cracks pasta out of the bowl like a finch, the tongs pull worms out of the flour like a robin, the teaspoon skims lettuce like a duck.
The straw looks useless until she sucks on it, caps the top with a finger and lifts one grain of rice. That is a hummingbird.
Ask her which beak she would want, then what a bird with tongs for a mouth does about the rice.
second.tip: Give her thirty seconds a go and count out loud. A time limit turns it into a game.

alternatives: Clothespins and pasta alone. One tool, one food, twenty minutes.
Feed the birds outside instead and watch which beak turns up.
Bury the worms in dry rice rather than flour and skip the mess.
Draw four beaks on paper and match them to birds in her book.
outAgain: Feeding the ducks, with oats or defrosted peas rather than bread
The pond edge, counting how many ducks tip up and how many dabble
A long walk with the stroller and no destination
The playground, for the tunnel and a run
The riverside path, looking for a heron standing still
days.krestonPM: He comes to the water in the carrier or the stroller and stays in one or the other the whole time you are near the edge. At 9 months ducks are the best moving thing he has seen all week. Hand Azlyn the food to show him.

insight.headline: Trying and failing at something an animal does easily builds real respect.
paras: Azlyn dropped the egg off her feet eleven times this morning. A penguin holds one there for two months. She learned more about that bird in ten minutes of failing at its job than she would from a photograph and a fact, because the difficulty went through her own ankles. Attempting an animal's movement gives a child a body-level measure of what the animal is doing, and the respect that comes out of it holds in a way that admiration does not. She will tell someone about the penguins this week, and the thing she tells them will be how hard it was.

days.safety: Dried pasta, uncooked rice and chunks of hard-boiled egg all end up on the floor today, and every one is a choking size for a 9-month-old who picks up single small things and mouths them. Sweep between activities rather than at the end, keep the bowls at the far side, and put him down on a floor you have looked at. Azlyn sucks in on the straw, so sit level with her and keep the rice bowl low. If she is a big inhaler, swap the rice for puffed cereal or drop the straw station. Count the string worms into the flour and count them back out, because a short length of string goes down him faster than the pasta does.

days.title: The Egg That Grows
days.prepTonight: The vinegar eggs have been working since Saturday night. If they only went in last night, rub the last of the shell off under the tap and carry on, and keep the bounce down to an inch because a thinner one bursts sooner. Put out the thick card, the paint, the measuring tape and January's handprint sheet for the afternoon.

opening.title: Rinsing Off the Shell
opening.need: the jar of vinegar eggs · 1 bowl of cool water · paper towels.
steps: The jar at the back of the counter holds the two raw eggs you covered with vinegar on Saturday night. Lift both out over the bowl. They are heavier than she expects and the shell has gone. A day and a half in vinegar ate it.
Rub the last white grit off under the water with your thumb. Let her do the second, flat hands, no fingers pushing.
Roll them dry on paper towels and let her hold one in two cupped palms. Ask what happened to the shell and leave her answer until 9:15.

main.title: The Egg With No Shell
materials: 2 raw eggs soaked 36 hours in a jar of white vinegar
Corn syrup, or 6 tablespoons of salt stirred into water
String and 1 pair of scissors (adult only)
1 sheet of card to tape the measured strings to
steps: Curtains shut. Hold the flashlight under one egg in her cupped hands. It lights up orange, the yolk a dark ball in the middle.
Bounce one from an inch above your open palm and let it land back in it. It gives and comes back. Two inches, no more: it is raw inside and will burst.
Wrap string round the fattest part of each egg, mark where it meets and cut there. You do the cutting. Tape both lengths to the card and write MONDAY beside them.
Fill one jar with plain water and the other with corn syrup. Label them with the marker and lower an egg into each.
Ask her which one will get bigger and write her answer on the card under the strings.
Both jars go on a high shelf where she can see them. She checks at 4:15, and you measure again with fresh string tomorrow.
main.tip: Water walks into the egg through its skin and syrup pulls it back out, so by tomorrow one is a water balloon and the other is wrinkled.

outside.title: The Same Gatepost
paras: Walk the New Year's Day route again and stop at the gatepost you have stopped at all winter. The first trees are breaking bud and most of the street is still bare. Put her hand flat on the same post and ask what has changed since the frost walk. Count the ones with green on them today, because in three weeks the count runs the other way.

days.infant: Kreston turns 10 months today. He cruises the sofa sideways, hand over hand, and points at what he wants instead of grabbing. On the walk, stop when he points and name the thing. Say happy ten months out loud, because nobody else will.

second.title: The April Handprint
second.intro: January's handprint sheet has been on the wall since Day 1. April's goes up next to it, and Kreston gets his first line on the door frame today.
materials: 1 wet washcloth in a shallow bowl
Poster putty, for putting the card up
January's handprint sheet, for the comparison
steps: Paint her palm with the wide brush rather than dipping her hand. Press flat on the left of the card, count to three, lift straight up. Write April and 3 in marker.
Kreston next on the same card beside hers, while he is calm and the washcloth is in your hand. Write 10 months under his.
Both of them against the door frame. Mark with the pencil, run the measuring tape from the floor and write the number and date on the wall. His first line lands four below hers.
Lay January's sheet next to April's and let her put her hand on both prints. She will do it twice.
Find January's pencil mark on the door frame and put her thumb on the gap. Three months, about the width of two fingers.
The card goes up on poster putty somewhere she passes, not into a drawer.
second.tip: Do her print first while your hands are clean, and keep the wet washcloth in the bowl beside you the whole time you are doing Kreston's.

alternatives: Handprints and nothing else. The wall marks can wait a day.
Draw round her whole hand in pencil instead of painting it.
Draw round her feet and compare those to January.
Measure everyone in the house, including the tallest and the teddy.
outAgain: The field walk, out to where the grass has come up since March
The footpath along the hedge, checking for nests in the low branches
The neighborhood park, for the swings and the run home
The lane, if there are lambs in anybody's field this week
days.krestonPM: He cruises the sofa and the coffee table now, so both egg jars come off any low surface once the measuring is done. At 10 months he understands no and stops, then checks your face. Put a low box of his own things where he cruises past.

insight.headline: Children can't perceive their own growth, and showing it matters.
paras: Azlyn cannot feel herself getting bigger. From the inside she has always been this size, so the January handprint under her April one is the first evidence she has ever had. Children build a sense of themselves through time out of external markers, and a three-year-old needs the marker to be physical: a hand that no longer fits, a pencil line she has passed, a coat from the winter. She will ask to check it, over and over. Keeping the sheets where she can reach them turns a craft activity into the thing she uses to answer her own question about growing up.

days.safety: The shell-less egg is raw inside and bursts if she grips it, so hands get washed with soap after every hold. Both jars go up high, because Kreston cruises furniture this month and pulls down whatever his hand lands on. The scissors stay with you.

days.title: Whose Egg Is Whose
days.prepTonight: Measure the two egg jars again before bed and tape the new strings up beside yesterday's. Put six sheets of paper, the ruler and one hen egg on the table, and the swimming bag by the door.

schedule.label: Quiet Play
schedule.name: The Paper Eggs on the Floor

opening.title: Six Eggs on One Sheet
opening.need: 1 sheet of paper · 1 pencil · 1 hen egg.
steps: Stand the hen egg on the paper and draw round it. That shape is the one she knows.
Ask her to draw the smallest egg she can imagine next to it, then the biggest that will still fit on the sheet.
Ask which bird lays each one. Take her answers and put the sheet aside. She finds out how close she got at 9:15.

main.title: From Hummingbird to Ostrich
materials: 1 pencil and 1 pair of child-safe scissors
1 quail egg, or a large dried lima bean as the stand-in
steps: Six sheets, one egg on each, drawn at true size with the ruler and the pencil: hummingbird 1 cm, robin 2 cm, quail 3 cm, hen 6 cm, goose 9 cm, ostrich 15 cm.
Trace the hen egg for the fourth and stand the quail egg (or the bean) on the third while you draw it.
She cuts out the four biggest with her child-safe scissors. You do the hummingbird and the robin, which are fiddly cuts.
Crayons, and she draws the bird beside each egg. Sizes out loud: a hummingbird sits in your palm, an ostrich is taller than Dad.
Lay all six along the hall floor smallest to biggest and tape them down against the baseboard.
Walk the line with her, the hummingbird end to the ostrich end and back. She will do it on her own nine more times before bed.
main.tip: One ostrich egg is worth around twenty-four hen eggs, and it takes an hour and a half to hard-boil.

outside.title: Birds From One Bench
paras: Pick a bench near a hedge, sit down and stay there for fifteen minutes. Count how many different birds land and name Sunday's tools by their beaks: the sparrow has a clothespin, the robin has tongs. Bring a handful of oats, let her put them out, then sit back down.

days.infant: Kreston is 10 months and has started pointing at what he wants you to look at. On the bench he points at movement before you spot it. Name whatever he picks out, right or wrong, then wait. He often points again to check you got the same one.

second.title: Feathers, Scales and Six Legs
second.intro: Her animal toys come out of the box and she sorts them by what the animal has on the outside.
materials: An old magazine or supermarket catalog
1 glue stick and 1 pair of child-safe scissors
4 sheets of paper or 4 paper plates
1 marker to draw the four headings
steps: Four sheets across the floor. Draw a heading on each with the marker: a feather, a patch of fur, a scale, a six-legged bug. Say the words and let her repeat them.
Tip the animals out. One at a time, she decides which sheet each one belongs beside.
Take the hard ones at face value. A penguin has feathers and does not fly. A whale has neither fur nor scales, and if she puts it with the fish, ask what it breathes.
When she gets stuck, hand her the animal and ask what her hand finds.
Magazine next. She cuts out any animal she can find with her child-safe scissors while you tear out the fiddly ones.
Glue each cutting onto the sheet she picks. Wrong ones stay where she put them.
Count each pile out loud and see which family won. Leave all four sheets out beside the toy box.
second.tip: Feathers and fur cut clean across color, so a brown bird and a brown dog land on different sheets.

alternatives: Two headings instead of four. Feathers and everything else.
Sort the toys by how many legs and stop there.
Find one of each family in her books rather than her toy box.
Sort the paper eggs from this morning by size again, then by bird.
outAgain: Swimming, and try her floating on her front with your hand under her chin
Indoor playground if the pool is closed for a school session
The library, a day early
A café with wet hair and something warm
The park on the way home, for twenty minutes of dry land
days.krestonPM: He comes to the pool, and twenty minutes in the water is plenty at 10 months. Hold him under the arms and walk him along the bottom. Dress him before yourself.

insight.headline: Sorting into families is a more advanced move than sorting by color.
paras: Color sits on the surface and Azlyn has been sorting by it since she was two. Feathers, fur and scales ask her to hold a rule the object does not show at a glance and apply it to a brown bird and a brown dog with different answers. That move, grouping by a property she has decided matters and ignoring the loud one, is the beginning of category thinking, and it runs underneath reading, number work and science. Her wrong answers are worth more than her right ones today, because a wrong one means she is using a rule rather than a memory.

days.safety: The quail egg, or the dried lima bean standing in for it, sits in a bowl on the far side of the table and goes away the moment the drawing is done. Both are a choking size for a 10-month-old, so neither goes on the floor and neither is left within Kreston's reach. The child-safe scissors stay at the table and come back to your hand between cuts. Poolside tile is wet, and Kreston pulls up on the steps and the rail without any idea of the drop, so one hand stays on him the whole time. Swimming this afternoon. Both children stay within arm's reach in the water at all times, and no float or seat is a substitute for your hands.

days.title: What the Wax Keeps Out
days.prepTonight: Boil six eggs and leave them in the fridge. Find the white crayon and a stub of white candle, and check there is vinegar left after Saturday.

schedule.label: The Main Event
schedule.name: The Lines the Dye Can't Cross

schedule.label: Quiet Play
schedule.name: The Dyed Eggs on the Table

opening.title: The Invisible Drawing
opening.need: 1 white wax crayon · paper, 2 sheets · 1 dark crayon with the paper peeled off.
steps: White crayon on white paper, pressing hard. She draws and the drawing vanishes as she makes it.
Lay the dark crayon on its side and rub it flat across the whole sheet. Her lines come back through the color.
Second sheet: she leaves you a message you cannot see, and you find it. Say nothing about why it works until 9:15.

main.title: The Lines the Dye Can't Cross
materials: 1 white wax crayon and a stub of white candle
Paper towels and 1 empty egg carton for drying
steps: Four mugs of hand-warm water, a teaspoon of vinegar in each, ten drops of a different color per mug. Stir with the slotted spoon handle.
She draws hard on the cold eggs with the white crayon. Nothing shows, so she works blind. Two get the candle stub, which lays a fatter line.
Lower two eggs into two different mugs with the slotted spoon. Three minutes for pale, six or seven for deep.
Lift the first out and roll it on paper towels. Every line she drew comes up white.
Dye the rest. Try one egg half in one mug and half in another, and one dipped, dried, crayoned again and dipped a second time.
Stand all six in the carton to dry, then on the table beside Friday's painted ones.
main.tip: Cold eggs take color slower and hold it better. If a mug comes out weak, another teaspoon of vinegar beats another ten drops of color.

outside.title: Water That Won't Soak In
paras: April gives you a wet sidewalk most days this week, so go out in it. Water beads and rolls off her coat, the hood of a car and the waxy top of an ivy leaf, and sinks into her jeans, the path and a paper bag. Let her tip a puddle onto a leaf and watch the drop sit up like a bead.

days.infant: Kreston is 10 months and cruises the furniture, which puts his hands at table height. The dye mugs stay at the far side of the table for the whole hour. Give him a plastic cup and a dry pastry brush at floor level, and he copies the brushing.

second.title: The Jar That Won't Mix
second.intro: Wax kept the dye off the shell this morning. Oil does the same to water, and this one she can shake.
materials: Vinegar, oil and a pinch of salt for the dinner dressing
1 small bottle or jar with a tight lid
steps: Half fill both jars with water, then half a cup of oil into each. The oil climbs to the top.
Lids on tight. She shakes the first jar hard and sets it down. Count while it comes apart again, about twenty seconds.
Two drops of food coloring into the first jar. The color falls through the oil and dyes the water underneath.
One teaspoon of dish soap into the second jar. Lid on, shake, and this one stays cloudy. Check both again after ten minutes.
The dressing next. Into the small bottle: three spoons of oil, one of vinegar, a pinch of salt. She shakes it until it goes thick and pale.
Put it in the fridge. At 4:00 it will have separated and she shakes it again for the table.
Ask her which jar the dressing is like.
second.tip: Dish soap works because one end of it grabs oil and the other grabs water. That is also why it gets the pan clean.

alternatives: One jar, no dish soap. Shake it and watch it split.
Drop cooking oil into a bowl of water and chase it with a spoon.
Wax crayon on paper and a watery paint wash over the top.
Float pepper on water and touch it with a soapy finger.
outAgain: Church hall playgroup, and take two dyed eggs to show and bring home
Indoor playground, if the hall is shut this week
The park with the shelter, for rain that has not stopped
The store, and let her carry one thing on the list
Home early with the eggs, if the morning has been enough
days.krestonPM: At playgroup he is a cruiser among crawlers and heads for the furniture rather than the mat, so find him a low bench to work along. He understands no this month and stops on it, which is worth saving for the door and the steps.

insight.headline: Resist techniques teach a real idea: some things repel others.
paras: The white crayon on the egg and the oil in the jar are the same fact twice. Wax and oil push water away, and Azlyn has now watched that happen on a shell, on paper, on her coat in the rain and in a jar she shook herself. A three-year-old builds a concept out of repeated instances in different materials rather than an explanation, and four in one day is a strong run at it. She will not have the word for it. She will have the expectation that water beads on some things and sinks into others, and the habit of checking which.

days.safety: Four mugs of hand-warm dye water sit at table-edge height today with a 10-month-old cruising the furniture and pulling down whatever his hand finds. Keep them past the middle of the table and empty them the moment the last egg is out. Vinegar stings in eyes, so wash her hands before she rubs her face, and food coloring stains everything it lands on.

days.title: Two Cooks, Two Pans
days.prepTonight: Stand both small frying pans on the cold stovetop with the oil, the soy and the sugar beside them. Check you have six eggs left.

schedule.label: Wind-Down
schedule.name: The Last Page of the Week

opening.title: Two Bowls, Two Forks
opening.need: 6 eggs · 2 bowls · 2 forks · soap at the sink.
steps: Three eggs into her bowl, three into yours. She has cracked a dozen since Saturday and is better at it.
A fork each, and beat until the yolk and the white are one color. Hers will have lumps and cook fine.
Both bowls into the fridge, both pairs of hands washed with soap. The pans come out at 9:15 and she gets her own.

main.title: Tamagoyaki, Twice
materials: 2 small non-stick frying pans, or one pan and take turns
steps: The two bowls of egg you both beat at 8:00 come out of the fridge, three eggs in each. A tablespoon of milk between them, half a teaspoon of soy each, the pinch of sugar split. She stirs hers with her fork.
Both pans on a low heat with a smear of oil. She stands beside you at the stovetop, your body between her and the burner, and you hold her pan handle throughout.
She pours a thin layer into her pan, enough to coat the bottom. Wait until the top stops looking wet.
Spatula in her hand with yours over it. Roll the sheet from the far edge toward you, push the roll back, oil the gap, pour the next layer in and lift the roll so the raw egg runs underneath.
Three or four layers each. Yours will be neater. Hers is a rolled omelette either way.
Tip both onto the board, let them sit a minute, then cut into thick slices onto the two plates. Count the layers in her slice.
main.tip: Low heat is the whole technique. A hot pan browns the layers so they stop sticking to each other, and the roll falls apart on the board.

outside.title: Chalk Eggs on the Path
paras: Take the chalk out to the path and draw Tuesday's six eggs again at sidewalk scale. The ostrich egg comes out as big as she is, and she can lie inside the outline. Draw the hummingbird one beside her thumb. Let her fill them in and leave the lot for the rain.

days.infant: Kreston is 10 months and copies what he sees hands doing. Sit him on the path with one fat piece of chalk and he bangs it, drags it, then looks at the mark. Keep it out of his mouth. Put him in the middle of the drawing.

second.title: The Book of What Happened
second.intro: Seven days of eggs, and she has forgotten Friday. A stapled paper book puts the week back in order, and you make one too.
materials: Your phone, for the week's photos
1 glue stick, for anything she wants stuck in
steps: Six sheets folded in half for each book, three staples down each spine. Let her push the stapler with your hand over hers. One book each.
Scroll the week's photos in order and name the days: painted eggs, books on shells, the penguin shuffle, the egg with no shell, six paper eggs, the dyeing, the pans.
One page per day. She draws first, and you write her sentence along the bottom in pencil, word for word.
Fill your own book at the same table and keep your hands off hers. She will look over.
Glue stick for anything she wants stuck in: a torn corner of yesterday's crayon sheet, one of Tuesday's small paper eggs.
Last page each. She names her favorite day and you write it down. Write yours in yours.
Swap books and read each other's back, out loud, cover to cover.
second.tip: Her sentence goes down as she says it. "The egg went bouncy" is the whole caption.

alternatives: One page, not seven. The best day of the week and nothing else.
Print six photos and let her put them in order on the floor.
Tell the week back to a grandparent on the phone instead.
Draw the whole week as one long picture across the back of a cereal box.
outAgain: The thrift store, with two dollars of her own to spend on a book
The bookstore window and the bakery next door, if the store is closed
The park, for a run before the store
The library, to hand back what came home last week
The bird feeder aisle at the garden center, after the week you have had
days.krestonPM: Take him into the thrift store in the carrier facing out. At 10 months he points at things across a room, so follow his finger. Let Azlyn choose a board book for him and carry it to the register.

insight.headline: Doing your own version beside her beats helping with hers.
paras: You cooked your own omelette this morning and made your own book this afternoon, and both times you left hers alone. That arrangement gives Azlyn a model she can watch without a correction attached to it. Children copy what they see competent adults doing and ignore most of what those adults tell them to do, so working next to her puts the whole demonstration on offer while the decisions stay hers. She also gets to see you make a mess of a layer and carry on, which is a harder thing to teach on purpose than any of the science this week.

days.safety: A hot pan and hot oil at stovetop height with a 10-month-old cruising toward the oven door. He stays out of the kitchen for the cooking hour, in the highchair or behind a gate, and every pan handle turns inward. The knife is yours for the slicing and goes back out of reach the moment the board is clear. Raw egg goes on her hands, the forks and the board, so soap and warm water before either child touches anything else.
